title: Town raises $108M to help your team operate at the speed of AI
content:
Town raises $108M to help your team operate at the speed of AI
Most of us remember that first magical moment when AI delivered an afternoon’s worth of work in a few minutes.
But work rarely ends at the individual. You need an updated model from finance, or for your ops lead to give you access to an app, or input from your field sales team to update next week’s targets, and progress is stalled while you wait for someone else to reply.
AI has made each of us faster on our own, but the work we do together hasn’t kept up. The more each of us can do, the more we are blocked by others. Our days fill up with waiting, and work slows down to a crawl again.
Building an Assistant for the Work We Do Together
We want AI to be as useful for the work we do together as it already is for the work we do on our own. To that end, we’re announcing our $108M Series B, co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures, with continued participation from a16z and First Round Capital, as well as Better Tomorrow Ventures, Precedent.vc, Scribble Ventures, Serena Ventures, Sparked Ventures, and notable angels, including Brendan Foody, Josh Silverman, Romain Huet, Scott Belsky, Steve Bartel, Taro Fukuyama, and Varun Anand.
“Townies that work together, so whole teams and organizations can move at the speed of AI.”
From day one, we’ve given each person a Townie who learns their people, projects, and voice, because an assistant can only help with what it understands. Thousands of businesses now rely on Townies to get work done every day.
That was the first step. Now we’re focused on the next one: Townies that work together, so whole teams and organizations can move at the speed of AI.
What AI Assistants Are Missing Today
Today your work assistant knows you, but it can’t work directly with your team. A team bot learns from team channels, but it can’t see anyone’s inbox or preferences, so it never really knows any one person. And in neither case can they work well with folks outside the company.
What if everyone had an assistant that understood the individual and the team? An assistant that understood what to keep private and what to share? An assistant that could handle the back-and-forth just like a human does by using the same emails, texts, and chat we do?
“Less of it waits on you, and you almost never wait on anyone else.”
This is what we’re building at Town.
Everyone gets their own Townie, and Townies work together. When the whole team has one, work starts to feel different. Less of it waits on you, and you almost never wait on anyone else.
Draft in anyone’s voice: Need an executive to step in? Your Townie works with theirs to draft the exact message in their style, so all they have to do is hit send.
Find a warm connection: Your Townie checks across the whole team to see who knows the person you’re trying to reach, asks for the intro, and books the meeting.
Pressure-test before meeting: Before you present, your Townie runs your draft past your teammates’ Townies to catch their biggest questions and fold in their feedback ahead of time.
Update once, apply everywhere: When a teammate improves a process or talking point, every Townie on the team adopts it instantly, so the efficiency gains reach everyone without the usual adoption curve.
Nobody had to schedule a meeting or wait for feedback. Each person made the call only they could make, and their Townies handled the rest.
A New Kind of Company Knowledge
Each of those moments works because Townies know you and your teammates: how the CEO writes, who has the strongest relationship with a buyer, what each lead cares about, the various processes that help run the business. Together, the Townies build a deep understanding of how your company actually runs, one that grows with every exchange.
“We believe that this context is a critical asset and should belong to the company that built it.”
Until Town, that context was trapped in individual heads and inboxes, disappearing whenever someone was too busy or left the company. Town turns that scattered context into a shared, compounding asset that helps your business thrive. Instead of slowing down as you scale, your company grows smarter and faster.
We believe that this context is a critical asset and should belong to the company that built it. That’s why if you ever leave Town, you can take it with you and use it anywhere.
The same respect for your business runs through the rest of Town. By default, none of your context is used to train a model. Town is SOC 2 Type 2 compliant, and our DPA is public, putting your business’ privacy and security first. And Town is provider-neutral. We don’t ask you to predict who will have the best or fastest or most cost-effective AI model in the coming years. Instead, we always use the appropriate AI model for each job, so you’re never locked into one provider and always get the right level of intelligence for the best price.
From Walking Alongside to Working Together
Earlier this year, we wrote about building an assistant who walks alongside you. One assistant can do a lot for one person, but we always meant it as a starting point.
The most important work a company does, it does together. Our hope is that by becoming part of how your team collaborates, Townies will transform what’s possible for your company.

report.summary: Town raised a $108M Series B to build collaborative AI assistants, called Townies, that coordinate across teams and turn company context into a shared asset.
report.background: AI productivity has mainly been individual: a person uses a chatbot or copilot to draft, analyze, or code faster. But most business work is collaborative, and gains stall when someone needs input, access, or approval from a colleague or partner. Existing team bots learn from shared channels but lack personal context; personal assistants know one user but cannot coordinate with others. Town previously offered each user a personal 'Townie' assistant. Its new funding, co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures with a16z, First Round Capital and angels, aims to connect those assistants into a team-wide layer. The company is betting that organizational context—how a CEO writes, who knows a buyer, which processes work—is a durable asset. It also emphasizes portability, privacy, and model neutrality as enterprises weigh multi-agent AI.
key_points: Town announced a $108M Series B co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures, with continued backing from a16z and First Round Capital plus several venture funds and angels. The round signals investor appetite for AI that improves team workflows, not just individual productivity.

The product shifts from one personal assistant per user to Townies that work together. They can draft messages in a colleague's voice, find warm introductions across the team, pressure-test presentations with teammates' assistants, and propagate process updates instantly—without scheduling meetings or waiting for replies.

Town treats company knowledge as a shared, compounding asset. Each exchange deepens the assistants' understanding of people, projects, and processes. If a customer leaves Town, it can export that context; by default, customer data is not used to train models.

Town stresses enterprise trust: SOC 2 Type 2 compliance, a public DPA, and provider neutrality. Rather than locking into one model vendor, it routes each job to the appropriate AI model for cost and capability. This positions Town between personal copilots and team-wide knowledge platforms.
report.impact: The raise points to a broader shift in enterprise AI from single-user copilots toward multi-agent coordination and shared context layers. For the AI industry, it validates that orchestration, memory, and governance may matter as much as raw model quality. For developers, Town's provider-neutral stance and context portability suggest demand for interoperable agent frameworks, secure memory stores, and audit trails. For regular users, the promise is less waiting on colleagues and fewer meetings, but also new questions about privacy: assistants that speak in your voice and share team knowledge must draw clear boundaries between personal and company data. Adoption will depend on trust, permissions, and whether Town can prove real productivity gains beyond demos.
report.tools: Watch Town itself, plus enterprise AI assistants such as Glean, Dust, Microsoft Copilot, and Slack AI for team-context approaches. Builders exploring multi-agent coordination can study open-source frameworks like CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen, and Letta (MemGPT) for agent memory. Also follow emerging standards for context portability, permissions, and model routing.
